newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: New Tajik peace deal could rekindle fighting.
newsitem.headline: New Tajik peace deal could rekindle fighting.

text.p: A peace deal aimed at ending Tajikistan's protracted and bloody civil war is fundamentally flawed, Western diplomats and observers said on Tuesday, warning that it could reignite conflict in the former Soviet republic.

Representatives of the Tajik government and their Islamist opponents meet in Moscow on Wednesday to work out military details of a peace accord agreed last December. Unlike earlier deals in a four-year war, the latest ceasefire has largely held.
"We think the talks will be successful," opposition representative Jaloleddin Makhmudov told Reuters. "We will also be discussing the legalisation of banned political parties."
But Western observers in the impoverished Central Asian republic say the two sides' inability to control armed bands who roam the mountain state may make the accord largely irrelevant.
"There might be a nice peace accord in Moscow but that does not mean peace on the ground," a senior aid worker said.
The remote territory bordering China and Afghanistan is divided into a motley array of mediaeval-style fiefdoms.

Opposition sources said some two dozen people may have died in a clash between rival warlords last week. Interfax news agency quoted another commander as threatening to "wipe out" rivals who took several foreigners hostage earlier this month.

Diplomats say a power-sharing deal struck in Iran last week, in which seats on a new commission for national reconciliation were shared out between the government and opposition, could be explosive because it leaves no places for any other faction.
The commission, to be chaired by opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri, is to implement the U.N.-sponsored peace accord. Beleaguered President Imomali Rakhmonov stays in his post.

"Tajikistan's various power blocks might not rise up in revolt," said a seasoned western diplomat in the capital, Dushanbe. "But neither will they feel any particular obligation to surrender their weapons and abide by the peace deal."
Yet again in Tajikistan's painful five years of statehood, peace on paper is at odds with grinding conflict on the ground.

"It might be hard to see it sometimes but this is a country at war," said the aid worker, whose trucks must to run the gauntlet of a confusing collection of armed bands to deliver aid to the country's weary population of 5.7 million. The latest scourge to hit them is a raging typhoid outbreak in Dushanbe.
Observers see a growing rapport between Nuri and Rakhmonov but say the fragile peace is also threatened by their more hardline lieutenants, unhappy with the treaty's compromises.
Nuri's return from Iran next month could provoke a violent reaction from those who feel left out of the peace deal.
"It wouldn't be hard to derail the peace," the diplomat said. "It would only take a few well-placed assassinations."
One armed group with major political clout -- the Russian Army -- is apparently loath to get entangled in Tajikistan's seething regional and clan rivalries.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, concerned the advance of the Taleban militia in Afghanistan could stir more trouble in former Soviet Central Asia, discussed joint security measures with his Tajik, Uzbek and Kyrgyz colleagues on Tuesday.
But, themselves frequent victims of attacks, some 20,000 Russian troops in Tajikistan are mostly confined to barracks.
"It's unfortunate but it's hard to be anything other than a hard-boiled pessimist here,' said an aid worker.
